title: Uniform compressed word problem for graph groups
formal: Is there a single deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple graph \((A,I)\) and a straight-line program \(S\) over \(A^{\pm1}\), decides whether \(\operatorname{val}(S)=1\) in the graph group \(G(A,I)=\langle A\mid ab=ba\text{ for }(a,b)\in I\rangle\)? The time bound must be polynomial in the combined encoded size of the graph and the program, uniformly over all graphs. This is the polynomial-time branch of the source question; membership in NP is its separate, weaker intermediate target.
context:
The source already uses polynomial-time compressed identity testing for each fixed graph group. Remark 10 identifies the missing uniform guarantee when the graph and alphabet also become input.

The expanded journal treatment proves a coRP upper bound in Theorem 3.12 while leaving deterministic polynomial time and NP membership open. The distinction is about the kind of efficient verification available, rather than basic decidability.

The 2024 paper solves the uniform power word problem for graph groups in polynomial time and obtains NP-completeness of their uniform uncompressed knapsack problem. Its introduction explicitly distinguishes the still-open arbitrary-SLP compressed word question.

Remark 10 explains that NP membership would suffice for an NP upper bound on solvability of compressed exponent equations when the graph group is input. That consequence involves SLP-encoded coefficients and is different from the later uncompressed knapsack result.
why: Asks whether efficient algebraic computation survives when both a compressed group element and the commutation structure of its ambient group vary. It isolates a uniformity obstacle that remains after fixed-group algorithms and more restricted compressed representations have been handled.
status_note: Read the conference definitions and Remark 10, the indexed primary author-manuscript Section 3.6, and the 2024 publisher full-text introduction. The old journal-manuscript PDF redirect prevented a local full download; journal dates were checked against publisher-deposited metadata. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of the uniform arbitrary-SLP question. The formal question explicitly selects P-membership and retains NP as a weaker branch, not an equivalent formulation.

definitions:
A graph group, also called a right-angled Artin group, has one generator for every vertex in A. An edge specifies that its two generators commute. I is symmetric and has no loops. The displayed presentation imposes these commutation relations and the group axioms, with no additional relations such as a²=1. The alphabet A±1 contains each generator and a formal inverse. Products are identified under insertion or deletion of adjacent inverse pairs and interchange of adjacent commuting letters, including their inverses. The identity is the class of the empty word. For instance aba⁻¹b⁻¹ is the identity when a and b are joined by an edge; without that edge, it is nontrivial in the two-generator free group.

A straight-line program is an acyclic sequence of string assignments. In a convenient normal form, X_i is assigned an alphabet letter, the empty word, or a concatenation X_jX_k with j,k<i. A designated final variable produces val(S). Reusing a variable means reusing its whole generated string; it does not introduce a new unknown group element. General finite right-hand sides can be put in this form with polynomial overhead. The expanded string can have exponential length in the program size and is not given explicitly.

Vertices and variables have binary indices. The graph is given explicitly, for example by its vertex and edge lists, and every program instruction is listed explicitly. Let L be the total bit length of this representation. The requested bound is L^{O(1)} bit operations on a deterministic machine, with one exponent and one algorithm for the entire input family. It cannot hide an arbitrary dependence on |A| or the commutation graph in a supposedly fixed constant. Equivalent explicit encodings differing by polynomial factors give the same P-membership question. Ill-formed graphs or cyclic programs may be rejected in polynomial time.

For the weaker NP question, every identity instance would need a certificate of length polynomial in L verifiable deterministically in polynomial time; nonidentity instances must have no accepting certificate. The known coRP result instead gives a randomized polynomial-time identity test that always accepts identities and accepts any nonidentity with probability at most 1/3. This does not by itself put identity instances in NP. The target concerns an arbitrary compressed word, not merely a product u₁^{z₁}⋯u_t^{z_t} of explicitly written words with given binary integer exponents, and not the existence of unknown exponents.
answer_criterion: Prove uniform deterministic polynomial-time decidability for arbitrary input commutation graphs and SLPs, or prove that no such algorithm exists, stating any complexity assumption used by a conditional obstruction. An NP upper bound is progress on the weaker branch and must not be reported as a positive answer to P-membership. A bound polynomial only for each fixed group, or an algorithm restricted to power words, does not settle this card.
